https://www.baltictimes.com/metrosert_in.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Metrosert Invests EUR 2 million in a Synthetic Biology Pilot Plant in Estonia 2026-07-22 Estonia’s Applied Research Centre and national metrology institute Metrosert has signed a contract worth nearly EUR 2 million with construction company Savekate OÜ to establish a unique synthetic biology pilot plant in Estonia. The new facility will provide biotechnology companies with a long-awaited opportunity to test and develop new production processes before making substantial investments in industrial-scale production. The pilot plant will serve both Estonian as well as international companies developing new products and ingredients from biological and renewable feedstocks. It will enable the production of proteins, enzymes, yeasts, plant-based fats and other bio-based substances used in food, materials, chemicals and pharmaceuticals to be developed and tested at a larger scale. Such technologies can help replace fossil-based raw materials while making production more resource-efficient and environmentally sustainable. According to Kaupo Reede, Head of Biorefining Unit at Metrosert’s Applied Research Centre, the pilot plant will provide Estonian biotechnology companies with a previously unavailable opportunity to progress from laboratory trials to production-ready solutions. “Synthetic biology is no longer a technology of the distant future, but a practical tool for building a new-generation economy. Estonia has a considerable number of entrepreneurs and researchers with strong ideas and promising initial laboratory results. To advance to the next stage, however, they need an environment in which technologies can be tested at a larger scale,” Reede said. According to Kaupo Reede, the absence of such a pilot facility has been a major bottleneck across the whole the region, preventing many biotechnology companies from successfully bringing their products into production. “Biotechnology is a capital-intensive and highly regulated field. Before industrial-scale production can begin, the process must be proven to work, its reliability must be assessed, and initial batches must be produced for prospective customers and partners to test. In most cases, it is neither feasible nor sensible for a company to build its own intermediate-scale facility for this purpose. The shared pilot infrastructure provided by Metrosert will help reduce development risks and bring solutions into actual production more quickly,” Reede explained. “The contract signed with Savekate OÜ is an important step towards ensuring that the ideas of Estonian entrepreneurs and researchers do not remain within laboratory walls but can reach production readiness in an environment that complies with international requirements. The pilot plant will serve as a bridge between science and commercial application,” he added. At the new pilot plant, companies will be able to develop their production processes, gradually scale up production volumes and manufacture their first larger product batches. Metrosert will also support companies in planning their development pathways, establishing international collaborative projects, and engaging partners and prospective customers. As the facility will also be used to develop and test solutions intended for the food industry and novel foods, it will be built to comply with stringent international food safety requirements. This will enable companies to develop processes and produce prototypes in an environment that supports their further progression towards industrial-scale production and international markets. Construction of Metrosert’s synthetic biology pilot plant will begin shortly, and the facility is expected to be completed by the end of 2026. About Metrosert AS Metrosert is Estonia’s national applied research centre and national metrology institute. The state-owned company employs approximately 140 specialists and supports sustainable economic growth through applied research, measurement and quality systems, as well as cooperation between industry and research institutions. The Applied Research Centre focuses on five areas: drone technologies, autonomous vehicles, hydrogen technologies, biorefining and health data. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images MMR Trump administration changes how it counts measles deaths amid Pennsylvania outbreak CDC announces changes to how it reports measles deaths as Pennsylvania continues to confirm more cases Melody Schreiber Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.35 BST Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.36 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Trump administration has changed the way it counts measles deaths amid an outbreak in Pennsylvania, which on Sunday saw the third apparent measles-related death in the state reported by a local coroner. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is now using data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), which is a way to track mortality trends over time, according to a note published to the agency’s website on 4 September. It’s a “puzzling” move, said Debra Houry, a former CDC chief medical officer. “The change doesn’t make any sense,” she added. This system is “not meant to confirm an individual case”; instead, it’s “usually focused on high-quality, long-term mortality trend analysis”, she said. Pennsylvania reports apparent third measles-related death amid outbreak Read more Previously, the CDC used a system called the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS), which the agency has described as the supply chain for data from local jurisdictions and states to the federal government. “CDC will report measles deaths if and when the National Center for Health Statistics reports measles as the underlying cause of death,” said Emily Hilliard, a US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) spokesperson. The CDC put an asterisk under its tally of deaths that leads to a note saying the NCHS “does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause”. Officials in Pennsylvania have confirmed two deaths this year, a newborn and a six-week-old infant, associated with measles. And a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson county, Pennsylvania, died on Saturday from probable measles, said Greg Furlong, the county’s coroner. The woman was unvaccinated and she had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with 24/7 oxygen support, both of which made her vulnerable to complications. The woman had not sought medical care for her apparent infection. “They were going to, but obviously got to the point where it turned to the worst and ultimately led to her death,” Furlong said. She had the classic measles rash and other symptoms, and a close contact had recently tested positive for measles. A nasal swab is undergoing testing for measles and results are expected within days. But the death will be classified as probable measles-related because of the epidemiological connection to a confirmed case, Furlong said. The woman would not have died without the measles case, despite her conditions, the coroner said. “None of us know when our last day is here on this Earth,” he said. “But I strongly 100% believe if this wouldn’t have come into her life that she would be alive today,” he said, adding: “Even with her underlying conditions, I believe she’d be alive today.” Maintaining a measles immunization rate of at least 95% is “absolutely” important for protecting people who are vulnerable to infection, Furlong said. That’s especially true for those who can’t be vaccinated, like infants under the age of six months and pregnant people. “We can all learn from this, and hopefully we can encourage more people who aren’t immunized to get immunized,” Furlong said, adding: “People do not want to be a statistic. “Hopefully this is something that more people get tested, more people get immunized. It’s something we thought we had eradicated, and here we are,” he said. “But it’s a shame that had to lead to somebody’s death.” Pennsylvania had 676 confirmed measles cases as of Friday, but Furlong said he believed the official case numbers are an undercount and there are more infections that are not being reported. “I 100% guarantee it,” he said. Furlong made the announcement on Sunday because “it’s informing people of something that we should all be aware of”, he said. Once the Pennsylvania department of health completes its investigation of the death, including the results from the nasal swab, it will notify the CDC of the case. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the HHS secretary, has not commented on the death, posting on X about fitness, Medicaid and Medicare fraud, and screen time. Kennedy previously argued without evidence that the two earlier deaths may not be from measles, and he asked Erica Schwartz, the CDC’s director, not to count the deaths in the official CDC tally, according to reporting by Reuters. The day after the Reuters report was published, the CDC changed its data source on measles deaths. Kennedy also spent nearly two decades at the helm of the Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organization, and he has repeatedly spread misinformation about vaccines. “CDC’s recommendation for the MMR vaccine has remained unchanged, and the Secretary has repeatedly said that the MMR vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent measles infection,” Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, said.
